sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Multidisciplinary Assessment
sections.description: The initial encounter with a pregnant patient presenting with atypical abdominal symptoms demands a high index of suspicion for pathology beyond the normal physiological changes of gestation. In this case, a nulliparous woman in her late forties presented in the second trimester (21 weeks) with severe, acute abdominal pain localized to the upper left quadrant and the pelvis, accompanied by mild dyspnea. While abdominal discomfort is common in pregnancy, the severity of the pain—quantified as a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) score of 5—and the association with respiratory distress signal a deviation from standard antenatal care. sections.section_title: Diagnostic Imaging Strategies and Safety Protocols
sections.description: The diagnostic evaluation of abdominal masses during pregnancy presents unique challenges due to the need to balance diagnostic accuracy with fetal safety. In the case of this 40-year-old primigravida presenting with severe abdominal pain and dyspnea in the second trimester, the initial imaging modality of choice was ultrasonography (US) with color Doppler. This approach serves as the primary screening tool because it is widely available, lacks ionizing radiation, and provides real-time visualization of fetal viability. In this specific scenario, US successfully identified two large, unilocular cystic masses with regular margins and confirmed peripheral vascularization. sections.section_title: Biochemical Markers and Differential Diagnosis Formulation
sections.description: The interpretation of serum tumor markers in pregnancy presents a unique diagnostic challenge due to profound physiological fluctuations that can mimic malignancy. In the case described, the patient's CA-125 level was elevated at 41.8 U/mL, exceeding the standard non-pregnant cutoff of 35 U/mL. While this might initially raise concern for epithelial ovarian carcinoma, understanding the natural history of CA-125 during gestation is paramount. Physiologically, CA-125 exhibits a biphasic pattern: it rises during the first trimester (peaking around 23 U/mL) and again in the third trimester (around 21 U/mL), typically dipping to a nadir of approximately 14 U/mL in the second trimester.
